Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 234 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2021)  
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 234 is located west of the Saskatchewan border, with Highway 14 to the north, 
Highway 41 to the west and Highway 13 to the south. The unit is approximately 2584 km2, and surrounds the eastern 
portion of the Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on its western border. The landscape within this WMU consists of 
private agricultural, private residential, public lands as grazing reserves, ecological and natural areas. 
 
The last aerial ungulate survey conducted in this unit was in 2015 and used the strip transect survey method.  The 
2015 population estimate was 4941 mule deer with a density estimate of 1.91/km2, 4268 white-tailed deer based on 
a density of 1.65/km2, and a population estimate of 1173 moose. Two hundred and eleven elk were observed during 
the survey  
 
The objective of the February 2021 aerial survey was to assess the current status of deer and moose populations 
within the WMU by determining estimates of population size, density, and age sex classes . We also recorded 
observations of additional species of interest, including carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or species at risk.  
 
Survey Method 
From February 2-4, 2021, a strip transect survey was conducted flying north-south lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) intervals 
with observations recorded for 200m on either side of the transect line (400m wide strip), resulting in 25% coverage, 
for a total linear survey effort of 1603 km (641 km2). Snow conditions were good with total coverage and some fresh 
snow. Sightability was excellent through most of the survey with some fog present and both sun and cloudy 
conditions. At each observation point, ungulates were counted by species, and  classified by sex and age  when 
possible.  
 
Sex a nd age classification were determined for moose by identification of vulva patch and size differential of 
cow/calves. However, due to timing of survey with respect to antler drop in deer, sex classification and distinguishing 
fawns from does was unreliable and large groups were left unclassified.  
 
Mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose densities were calculated following Jolly 1969 (as described in Krebs 2014) 
for surveys conducted with unequal sized units without replacement because the transect lengths varied. Density 
was multiplied by WMU area to determine population estimates. A correction factor of 90% for deer detectability was 
applied to population and density estimates (Habib et al. 2012), with a factor of 95% applied to moose density and 
population estimates. Elk observations were recorded during the survey, but population estimates were not 
calculated because the design of this survey is not appropriate for elk population calculation. Elk were considered a 
minimum count.  
 
Results 
In total  939 white -tailed deer were observed in 193 groups , only 40% of the white -tailed deer observed were 
classified, 8% were bucks, 18% were does and 14% were fawns. The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.44, and 
0.76 respectively, but were influenced by antler drop and limited classification. The estimated abundance for white-
tailed deer is 4163, for a density of 1.61/km2 (Table.1).  
 
There were 1251 mule deer observed within 197 groups, 50% of the deer observed were classified, 15% were bucks, 
19% were does, and 16% were fawns. The buck:doe ratio and fawn:doe ratio were 0.79, and 0.85 respectively, but 
again were influenced by antler drop and its influence on proper classification.  The estimated abundance of mule 
deer is 5547 individuals, with a density of 2.15 /km2 (Table 2).

Two hundred and seventy seven moose were observed within 145 groups. Of the 277 moose identified, 68 (28%) 
were bulls, 99 (40%) were cows, 73 (30%) were calves and 7 (3%) were not classified. The bull:cow ratio was 0.69 
and the calf:cow ratio was 0.74 (Table 3).  Moose population was estimated at 1172 individuals, and the average 
moose density was estimated at 0.45/km2 (Table 3).   
 
Lastly, there were 272 elk observed within 29  groups, of the 272 elk identified, 21 (8%) were bulls , 25 (9%) were 
cows, 19 (7%) were calves, and 207 (76%) were not classified. Incidental observations were also noted during the 
survey,  117 coyotes, 161 Sharp-tailed grouse, 20 Gray Partridges, 2 snowshoe hares, 2 pileated woodpeckers 2 
red fox, 2 porcupines, 1 Great-horned Owl, 1 Ruffed grouse, and 1 Bald Eagle, these should not be considered 
minimum total counts.
